newsitem.title: INDIA: India's economic growth seen hurting environment.
newsitem.headline: India's economic growth seen hurting environment.

text.p: India needs curbs to prevent economic development from inflicting serious damage to the environment, several government ministers cautioned on Wednesday.
Finance Minister P.Chidambaram, speaking at a seminar, said India's economy was expected to grow by seven percent in 1997/98 (April-March) and was aiming at sustaining eight percent growth.

To achieve this without harming the environment, India needed market-oriented energy prices, community support for the environment and government action to regulate the use of natural resources and punish environmental offenders, he said.
"In each of these (spheres) the state is weak and indecisive," Chidambaram said. "If we must sustain development over the next 50 years, we must address each of these concerns."
Experts at the seminar, organised by the independent Tata Energy Research Institute (TERI), were working to set a 50-year agenda for environmentally sustainable economic development.

"If India and China reach the per-capita income levels of even a quarter of developed countries, even with an optimistic outlook on technology, the world is unsustainable," Junior Power Minister Yogendra Alagh told the seminar.

Last year, the World Bank estimated India's annual per-capita income in 1994, adjusted for domestic prices, at $1,280. China's income was $2,510. The comparable figures were $25,880 for the United States and $21,140 for Japan.
TERI said in a background paper for the seminar that India's recent success in growing enough food for its people had caused adverse side-effects.
"It has been at the cost of falling water tables, degrading soils, poor management of irrigation systems and the harmful side-effects of increasing pesticide and fertiliser use," it said.
"Industrial growth, urbanisation and the spread of intensive agriculture generate increasing wastes, which pollute India's rivers, air and land," it said.
TERI said it estimated India's per capita water availability to fall to 1,600 cubic metres a year in 2017 from 2,300 cubic metres in 1997.
Gradual soil degradation is expected to cause an economic loss of at least 89 billion rupees ($2.5 billion) in 1997.
Municipal solid waste generated in Indian cities had swelled to 48 million tonnes by 1997, compared to six million tonnes in 1947, TERI said.
"India is in a very bad shape, I must admit," Environment Minister Saifuddin Soz said. "There is tremendous pressure on forests and wildlife."
TERI director R.K. Pachauri said a delay in easing state control and implementing market prices for electricity had encouraged inefficient use of degradable resources.
